stem: What is the key difference between AWS Systems Manager Run Command and Systems Manager Automation?

choices.text: Automation targets only on-premises servers; Run Command only EC2
Run Command runs ad hoc commands; Automation orchestrates multi-step workflows
Run Command requires a Lambda function to execute, while Automation doesn't
They are the same feature under two different console menu names

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Run Command runs commands ad hoc on instances. Automation orchestrates multi-step workflows across AWS resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Target restrictions: no.
• Run Command requires Lambda: no.
• Same feature: no.

Key takeaway: one-off commands vs. orchestrated runbooks.

stem: A CloudOps engineer must ensure that a specific antivirus agent configuration and a required set of registry settings remain applied on a fleet of managed EC2 instances on an ongoing basis, automatically correcting any instance that drifts from the desired state. Which Systems Manager capability is designed for this?

choices.text: Systems Manager State Manager
Systems Manager Distributor
Systems Manager Session Manager
Systems Manager Automation with a one-time execution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
State Manager associations continuously apply and maintain a desired configuration on instances on a schedule.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Distributor: package distribution.
• Session Manager: shell access.
• One-time Automation: not continuous.

Key takeaway: keep instances in desired state → State Manager.

stem: An Automation execution using the AWS-managed document AWS-RestartEC2Instance fails at a step with the error AccessDenied when attempting to call ec2:RebootInstances. The engineer manually has permission to reboot the instance in the console. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The OS blocks the API call at the network layer
Automation always uses root account credentials and can't be denied
The Automation role lacks ec2:RebootInstances
AWS-RestartEC2Instance is deprecated and no longer works in any Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Automation execution role lacks ec2:RebootInstances, so that step fails with access denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OS blocks API: no.
• Root credentials: no.
• Deprecated document: no.

Key takeaway: Automation failures → execution role permissions.

stem: The team wants Lambda to run whenever an EC2 instance changes state, a SaaS partner sends an event, or a nightly schedule fires, with filtering on event content. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SNS
Amazon SQS
AWS Step Functions
Amazon EventBridge

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge receives AWS service events, SaaS partner events, and custom events, filters them with patterns, supports schedules, and routes to targets such as Lambda.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS: pub/sub messaging, with no native AWS service event bus or SaaS partner sources.
• SQS: a queue, not event routing.
• Step Functions: orchestration, not event ingestion.

Key takeaway: event routing from many sources → EventBridge.

stem: A CloudOps engineer wants to automatically tag every newly launched EC2 instance with the name of the IAM principal that launched it, without requiring developers to change their launch process. Which event-driven approach accomplishes this?

choices.text: An S3 bucket notification that fires whenever an instance starts
EventBridge on RunInstances triggering a tagging Lambda
Ask developers to add a required tag field in the launch wizard
An hourly Run Command that tags any untagged instances it finds

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on the RunInstances CloudTrail event triggers a Lambda function that tags each new instance with the creator's identity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 notification: unrelated to EC2.
• Launch wizard field: unreliable.
• Hourly Run Command: delayed.

Key takeaway: auto-tag on creation → EventBridge + CloudTrail event.

stem: A CloudOps engineer needs an S3 upload to trigger a workflow that involves matching against multiple content-based filters and routing to several different targets, including a Step Functions state machine and an SNS topic, with the ability to archive and replay events later. Compared to configuring S3 bucket notifications directly, what is an advantage of enabling EventBridge notifications on the bucket instead?

choices.text: Direct S3 notifications support more target types than EventBridge
EventBridge adds rich filtering, multi-target fan-out, and replay
Direct S3 notifications retain a 90-day replay log by default
EventBridge cannot be used with S3, only with EC2 and CloudTrail events

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sending S3 events to EventBridge adds rich filtering, multiple targets per rule, and archive and replay.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Direct notifications more targets: fewer.
• 90-day replay by default: no.
• EventBridge can't use S3: it can.

Key takeaway: complex S3 event routing → EventBridge.

stem: An EventBridge rule targets a Lambda function to remediate noncompliant security group changes, but CloudWatch metrics show the rule is matching events successfully while the Lambda function's invocation count remains at zero. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The function's runtime has been deprecated by AWS
The rule's event pattern is too broad and matches too many events
The function policy doesn't allow EventBridge to invoke it
The function's memory is too low to start execution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the rule matches but the function never runs, the function's resource-based policy may not allow EventBridge (events.amazonaws.com) to invoke it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deprecated runtime: different error.
• Too broad pattern: would over-trigger.
• Low memory: function would still start.

Key takeaway: EventBridge → Lambda needs invoke permission.

stem: Alarms for RDS, EC2, and Lambda issues should create tracked operational issues with context, related resources, suggested runbooks, and status, deduplicated, rather than scattered emails. Which capability fits?

choices.text: Systems Manager OpsCenter OpsItems
AWS Config rule notifications
SNS topics with email subscriptions
CloudWatch dashboards

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpsCenter creates OpsItems from alarms and events, with related resources, runbook suggestions, status tracking, and deduplication.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SNS email: no tracking or context.
• Dashboards: visualization, not issue tracking.
• Config notifications: compliance only.

Key takeaway: track operational issues → OpsCenter.

stem: A scheduled EventBridge rule using a cron expression is intended to invoke a Systems Manager Automation runbook every day at 6:00 AM UTC to stop nonproduction EC2 instances, but the rule has never triggered the runbook. The rule shows as enabled and its event pattern section is empty since it is schedule based. What should the engineer check next?

choices.text: Whether the S3 bucket policy allows EventBridge to read objects
Whether the rule's cron expression uses local time instead of UTC, since EventBridge only accepts local time zones
Whether the target EC2 instances have the Systems Manager Agent uninstalled
Whether the IAM role attached to the EventBridge rule has permission to call ssm:StartAutomationExecution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge needs an IAM role with permission (for example, ssm:StartAutomationExecution) to start the Automation runbook target.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 bucket policy: unrelated.
• Local time cron: EventBridge rules use UTC, but the rule fires; the target fails.
• SSM Agent: only for commands on instances.

Key takeaway: rule targets need role permissions.

stem: After a recurring incident where developers accidentally leave large, unattached Amazon EBS volumes provisioned, a CloudOps engineer wants to automatically identify and delete unattached volumes older than 7 days every night, with an approval step required before deletion in production accounts. Which approach best satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: A scheduled runbook with an approval step
Use AWS Budgets to alert when EBS costs increase
Review the EC2 console manually every night before leaving
An S3 lifecycle policy deleting snapshots older than 7 days

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A scheduled Automation runbook with an approval step finds unattached volumes and deletes them only after approval.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Budgets alert: no cleanup.
• Manual nightly review: toil.
• S3 lifecycle: EBS isn't S3.

Key takeaway: safe automated cleanup → runbook with approval.

stem: A CloudOps team uses Amazon DevOps Guru to detect operational anomalies in their serverless application. They want any new DevOps Guru insight to automatically create a ticket in their incident management system and, for a specific known issue pattern, trigger a Systems Manager Automation runbook to remediate it without waiting for a human to check the DevOps Guru console. Which architecture enables this?

choices.text: EventBridge rules on DevOps Guru insights to Lambda and SSM
Poll the DevOps Guru API every minute with a cron job on EC2
Write insights into RDS and use database triggers to invoke Lambda
A built-in DevOps Guru auto-remediation that runs SSM runbooks directly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge rules on DevOps Guru insight events can route to Lambda or SSM runbooks for automated responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Polling API with cron: inefficient.
• RDS triggers: overcomplicated.
• Built-in auto-remediation: not a DevOps Guru feature.

Key takeaway: act on insights → EventBridge.

stem: An account must enforce passwords of at least 14 characters with symbols, prevent reuse of the last 5, and expire them every 90 days for IAM users. Which control fits?

choices.text: An SCP requiring strong passwords
An AWS Config rule that resets weak passwords
IAM Identity Center MFA settings
An IAM account password policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The IAM account password policy sets length, character requirements, reuse prevention, and expiration for IAM user passwords.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCP: controls API permissions, not password rules.
• Config: can evaluate the policy but doesn't enforce passwords.
• Identity Center MFA: a different identity store and control.

Key takeaway: IAM user password rules → account password policy.

stem: Security requires MFA for root and every console user, with phishing-resistant keys for administrators. Some admins want to share one security key. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: One virtual MFA app can be assigned to several users at once
MFA can be enabled for the root user only
Keys can be registered per user; each MFA device belongs to one identity
IAM MFA automatically satisfies Cognito app logins

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM supports virtual, FIDO security key, and hardware TOTP devices. An MFA device is assigned to one IAM identity (a user can have several devices), so admins shouldn't share one device.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One device for several users: not supported.
• Root only: IAM users can use MFA too.
• Cognito: separate user pools.

Key takeaway: one device per identity; prefer FIDO keys for admins.

stem: A CloudOps engineer notices that a CloudTrail trail's log files stored in Amazon S3 may have been tampered with after delivery. Which CloudTrail feature should be enabled to detect whether a log file has been modified or deleted after it was delivered?

choices.text: Log file integrity validation
CloudTrail Lake
Server-side encryption with SSE-KMS on the trail
CloudTrail Insights

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Log file integrity validation uses signed digest files to detect whether log files were modified or deleted.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail Lake: querying.
• SSE-KMS: encryption, not tamper detection.
• Insights: anomalies.

Key takeaway: tamper detection → integrity validation.

stem: The team wants continuous findings for any S3 bucket, KMS key, or IAM role that grants access to principals outside its AWS Organization. Which service fits?

choices.text: GuardDuty findings for unusual S3 API calls
Amazon Macie findings for publicly accessible buckets
IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust
Trusted Advisor checks for S3 bucket permissions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Access Analyzer evaluates resource policies (S3, KMS, IAM role trust, and others) and reports access granted outside the chosen zone of trust, such as the organization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: limited checks, mainly public buckets.
• Macie: data classification (with some bucket posture), not cross-account policy analysis for keys and roles.
• GuardDuty: behavior, not policy analysis.

Key takeaway: external access via policies → Access Analyzer.

stem: A developer reports that an application using an IAM role cannot call the ec2:DescribeInstances action, even though the attached policy appears to allow it. The CloudOps engineer wants to test the effective permissions of the role for this specific action before making any changes. Which tool should be used first?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail Lake query
The IAM Policy Simulator
AWS Config rule evaluation history
Amazon Inspector network reachability analysis

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The IAM Policy Simulator evaluates policies for a principal and action to show whether and why access is allowed or denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail Lake: history.
• Config history: configuration.
• Inspector reachability: network.

Key takeaway: debug permissions → Policy Simulator.

stem: A company is restructuring its multi-account AWS environment using AWS Organizations. It wants production workloads and development workloads to have different sets of guardrails, while still allowing centralized billing and consolidated CloudTrail logging across all accounts. What is the best way to organize the accounts?

choices.text: Use IAM Identity Center permission sets instead of Organizational Units to separate production and development guardrails
Create a separate AWS Organization for production and another for development
Place all accounts directly under the organization root and apply one SCP to the entire organization
Create separate organizational units for production and development, and attach different SCPs to each OU

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Separate OUs for production and development let different SCPs and guardrails apply to each.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity Center instead: different purpose.
• Separate organizations: extra overhead.
• All under root: no differentiation.

Key takeaway: environment separation → OUs.

stem: An admin assigns the 'ReadOnlyOps' permission set to a group for 30 accounts. What is created in each account, and how do users get access?

choices.text: A resource policy added to every resource in each account
An IAM role from the set; users assume it through the access portal
An SCP attached to each of the 30 accounts in the organization
An IAM user per group member, each with long-term access keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Identity Center provisions an IAM role from the permission set in each assigned account. Users sign in to the access portal and get temporary credentials for that role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM users: Identity Center doesn't create users with keys.
• SCP: a separate Organizations feature.
• Resource policies: not how permission sets work.

Key takeaway: permission set → role per account → temporary credentials.

stem: The team wants an automated weekly check across all accounts for root MFA, security groups open to the world, and exposed access keys, with Business Support. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector network reachability
AWS Trusted Advisor with organizational view
Amazon Detective
AWS Config manual rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor security checks include root MFA, unrestricted security group ports, and exposed access keys. Business Support and higher unlock all checks, and organizational view aggregates results.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: vulnerabilities and reachability of workloads.
• Config manual rules: would need custom setup for each check.
• Detective: investigation, not checks.

Key takeaway: broad baseline checks → Trusted Advisor.

stem: A CloudOps team must demonstrate compliance with an internal security baseline across dozens of AWS accounts by grouping multiple related AWS Config rules together and deploying them consistently through AWS Organizations. Which AWS Config feature should be used?

choices.text: A conformance pack
A single custom Config rule with multiple Lambda triggers
A Config recorder with multiple delivery channels
An aggregator authorization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A conformance pack bundles Config rules and remediations to demonstrate compliance with a baseline and can be deployed across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One custom rule: not a baseline.
• Multiple delivery channels: not supported this way.
• Aggregator authorization: data collection.

Key takeaway: compliance baselines → conformance packs.

stem: A company operates in multiple AWS Regions and wants a single CloudTrail configuration that automatically captures management events from every current and future Region into one Amazon S3 bucket, rather than creating a separate trail per Region. What should the engineer configure?

choices.text: AWS Config aggregators configured in each Region
A separate trail per Region, each delivering to its own bucket
A single multi-Region trail
CloudTrail Insights enabled globally with no trail required

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A single multi-Region trail logs events in all Regions, including new ones, to one destination.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config aggregators: not CloudTrail.
• Per-Region trails: more work.
• Insights without a trail: requires a trail.

Key takeaway: all Regions → multi-Region trail.

stem: Operations must see at a glance which S3 buckets hold confidential data, and access policies and backups should follow automatically from that classification. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A spreadsheet of classifications kept outside AWS
Classification tags that drive policies and automation
Bucket names that include confidential or public
Different storage classes for each sensitivity level

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tags such as data-classification=confidential are machine-readable. IAM (tag-based conditions), AWS Backup (tag-based selection), and automation can act on them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Names: can't be changed easily, and policies can't rely on them well.
• Spreadsheet: disconnected from enforcement.
• Storage classes: about cost and access, not sensitivity.

Key takeaway: classification as tags enables automated controls.

stem: An ACM certificate using DNS validation has been Pending validation for two days. The domain's DNS is hosted by a third party. What must be done, and what keeps renewals automatic?

choices.text: Add ACM's CNAME at the DNS host and keep it for renewals
Transfer the domain's DNS to Route 53 permanently
Approve the email ACM sends to the domain's WHOIS contact
Upload the private key from an existing CA to ACM

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS validation requires creating the CNAME record ACM provides at whichever DNS provider hosts the zone. Leaving it in place lets ACM renew automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Email: that's the email validation method.
• Private key upload: not part of issuance.
• Route 53: convenient but not required.

Key takeaway: DNS validation = CNAME, kept in place.

stem: After enabling automatic rotation for a database secret in AWS Secrets Manager, an application begins receiving authentication failures immediately after each rotation cycle. What is the most likely cause the CloudOps engineer should investigate first?

choices.text: KMS rotation is disabled for the default aws/secretsmanager key
The rotation function can't reach or update the secret and the database
The application uses an IAM role instead of a database username and password
Secrets Manager does not support rotation for database credentials

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If rotation fails, the rotation function may not reach the secret endpoint or database, or lacks permission to update the password, leaving mismatched credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• KMS rotation: unrelated.
• IAM role vs. username: unrelated.
• No DB rotation support: supported.

Key takeaway: rotation failures → function network and permissions.

stem: An Amazon GuardDuty finding indicates UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce for an EC2 instance. What does this finding type indicate, and what is an appropriate first response action?

choices.text: Repeated failed SSH logins from a suspicious source; tighten SGs
The instance role has excessive permissions and needs a boundary
The instance is missing a Config conformance pack
The root volume is unencrypted and needs EBS encryption
CloudTrail logging has stopped and the trail must be re-enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SSHBruteForce means repeated failed SSH logins from a suspicious source. Tighten SSH access (restrict or remove port 22, use Session Manager).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Excessive role permissions: different finding.
• Missing conformance pack: unrelated.
• Unencrypted volume: unrelated.
• Trail stopped: different finding.

Key takeaway: brute force → restrict SSH exposure.

stem: Operations wants GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config findings in one normalized view across 20 accounts, with scores against AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Detective
AWS Audit Manager
AWS Security Hub
Amazon Security Lake

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security Hub aggregates and normalizes findings (ASFF) from services such as GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config, and runs security standards such as FSBP with scores, across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Detective: investigation of findings.
• Audit Manager: evidence for audits.
• Security Lake: a data lake of logs for analytics, not a findings dashboard with standard scores.

Key takeaway: one findings view + standard scores → Security Hub.

stem: A team wants to know which EC2 instances have critical CVEs AND are reachable from the internet, to fix those first. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon GuardDuty
VPC Flow Logs analysis
Amazon Inspector (CVEs with network reachability)
AWS Trusted Advisor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector finds software vulnerabilities and evaluates network reachability, factoring exposure into its risk score so internet-reachable critical findings rank highest.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty: threat detection.
• Trusted Advisor: open ports checks, but no CVEs.
• Flow logs: traffic, not vulnerabilities.

Key takeaway: prioritize vulnerabilities by exposure → Inspector.

stem: After adding a new NACL rule to explicitly deny inbound traffic from a malicious IP range on a subnet, legitimate clients outside the VPC suddenly cannot complete TCP connections to instances in that subnet, even though the deny rule has a higher (later evaluated) rule number than existing allow rules. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: NACL rules are evaluated in random order
NACLs can't contain both allow and deny rules in the same rule set
The deny's lower rule number blocks ephemeral return traffic
The security group on the instances is now blocking the traffic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACL rules are evaluated lowest number first. A broad deny at a lower number can also block ephemeral return traffic for legitimate flows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Random order: no.
• Can't mix allow and deny: they can.
• Security group now blocking: unchanged.

Key takeaway: check what a new NACL deny actually matches.

stem: Instances must be blocked from resolving known malware domains using an AWS-managed list, and blocked queries must be logged. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Security groups that deny outbound port 53
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall with query logging
A private hosted zone containing each malicious domain
GuardDuty findings acting as the blocking control

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall filters queries at the VPC resolver using managed or custom domain lists with BLOCK actions, and Resolver query logging records the queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG on port 53: would break all DNS.
• Private zones for bad domains: can't keep up with changing lists and isn't a policy tool.
• GuardDuty: detects, doesn't block.

Key takeaway: domain blocking at the resolver → DNS Firewall.

stem: A company wants deep packet inspection and intrusion prevention capabilities (such as signature-based threat detection) applied to traffic flowing between its VPC and the internet, beyond what security groups and NACLs provide. Which AWS service should be deployed?

choices.text: AWS Shield Standard
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Network Firewall
AWS WAF

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Network Firewall provides stateful inspection and intrusion prevention with Suricata-compatible signatures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Standard: DDoS.
• GuardDuty: detection.
• WAF: HTTP-layer filtering.

Key takeaway: VPC IPS → Network Firewall.

stem: Two EC2-based endpoints must receive DNS traffic 70/30 for an A/B test, and an endpoint should be removed from answers if its health check fails. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Multivalue answer records for both endpoints
Latency records for both endpoints
Failover records with the 30% endpoint as secondary
Weighted records (70/30) with health checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weighted routing returns records in proportion to their weights, and associated health checks exclude unhealthy endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency: routes by network performance, not proportions.
• Failover: all traffic to the primary until it fails.
• Multivalue: returns several healthy records but no set proportions.

Key takeaway: traffic percentages in DNS → weighted records.

stem: A global SaaS company has application stacks deployed in the us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1 regions. It wants each user's DNS query to be answered with the record for whichever regional endpoint currently provides the fastest round-trip response for that user, and to automatically shift if network conditions change. Which Route 53 routing policy best satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Geolocation routing based on the user's country
Latency-based routing across records in all three regions
Multivalue answer routing
Simple routing with a single record listing all three IP addresses

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Latency-based routing sends each user to the Region with the lowest latency among the three.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Geolocation: by country, not performance.
• Multivalue: random healthy answers.
• Simple with three IPs: no latency awareness.

Key takeaway: best performance globally → latency routing.

stem: A media company must ensure that users located in a specific country are directed only to a compliance-approved regional endpoint that stores their data locally, per local regulation, regardless of which endpoint would be fastest for them. Which Route 53 routing policy should be configured?

choices.text: Latency-based routing
Multivalue answer routing
Geolocation routing
Weighted routing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Geolocation routing directs users by country to a specific endpoint, meeting compliance requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency: may route elsewhere.
• Multivalue: random.
• Weighted: proportional.

Key takeaway: country-based routing → geolocation.

stem: After an incident, security needs to know which instances looked up a suspicious domain last week, with the source IP and response. Which log source fits?

choices.text: Route 53 Resolver query logs
CloudTrail management events
VPC Flow Logs
ALB access logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resolver query logging records DNS queries made from VPC resources, including the query name, source IP, instance ID where available, and response code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: exclude traffic to the Amazon DNS resolver.
• CloudTrail: AWS API calls, not DNS lookups.
• ALB logs: HTTP requests to the load balancer.

Key takeaway: who resolved what → Resolver query logs.

stem: A company has an on-premises data center connected to its AWS VPC via AWS Direct Connect. It needs resources in the VPC to resolve DNS names hosted on on-premises DNS servers, and it also needs on-premises servers to resolve names in a Route 53 private hosted zone associated with the VPC. What should be configured?

choices.text: Outbound endpoint with forwarding rules plus an inbound endpoint
A public hosted zone shared with the on-premises network over the internet
A single outbound endpoint, with nothing else needed for on-prem-to-VPC queries
Direct Connect handles DNS in both directions without Resolver endpoints

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An outbound endpoint with forwarding rules resolves on-premises names from the VPC, and an inbound endpoint lets on-premises DNS resolve AWS private names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zone: exposure.
• Outbound only: one direction.
• DX handles DNS: no.

Key takeaway: bidirectional hybrid DNS → inbound + outbound endpoints.

stem: A company serves its website through Amazon CloudFront with a single origin, an Application Load Balancer in one AWS Region. To improve availability if the primary origin becomes unhealthy, the company wants CloudFront to automatically serve requests from a secondary origin in another Region without requiring a DNS change. What should be configured?

choices.text: An origin group with status-code-based failover
Route 53 failover pointing directly at the ALB, bypassing CloudFront
One origin with a custom error page redirecting to the other Region
Two distributions with a weighted Route 53 record between them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A CloudFront origin group with status-code-based failover switches to a secondary origin when the primary fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 to ALB: bypasses CloudFront.
• Custom error redirect: clunky.
• Two distributions: complex.

Key takeaway: CloudFront origin failover → origin groups.

stem: The zone apex example.com must point at a CloudFront distribution, and the company wants no charge for these queries and automatic tracking of CloudFront's IPs. Which record fits?

choices.text: A records containing CloudFront's current IPs
An MX record pointing to the distribution
A CNAME record at the apex pointing to CloudFront
Route 53 alias A/AAAA records to the distribution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Alias records are allowed at the zone apex, follow the target's changing IPs, and queries to aliases for AWS resources such as CloudFront are free.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CNAME at apex: not allowed by DNS rules.
• Hardcoded IPs: CloudFront IPs change.
• MX: mail routing.

Key takeaway: apex + AWS target → alias.

stem: An engineer configured a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule to send queries for corp.example.internal to an on-premises DNS server over a Direct Connect connection. EC2 instances in the VPC still fail to resolve names in that domain. Security groups on the outbound endpoint allow outbound DNS (port 53) to the on-premises DNS server IP, and the rule is confirmed present. What should the engineer check next?

choices.text: Whether a public hosted zone exists for corp.example.internal
Whether the instances have public IP addresses assigned
Whether CloudFront is configured for the domain
Whether the rule is associated with the instances' VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Resolver forwarding rule applies only to VPCs it's associated with. Check that the rule is associated with the instances' VPC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public zone: not needed.
• Public IPs: not needed.
• CloudFront: unrelated.

Key takeaway: rules must be associated with VPCs.

stem: One instance in a public subnet with a public IPv4 address can't reach the internet, while others in the same subnet can. The subnet routes to an IGW. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether the VPC has a peering connection to another VPC
Whether Shield Advanced is enabled on the account
Whether a gateway VPC endpoint was created for S3
Its SG, OS firewall, and routes; subnet-wide causes are ruled out

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Because other instances in the same subnet work, the route table and NACL are likely fine. The difference is instance-specific: its security groups, OS firewall, OS routes, or a missing public IP association.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Peering, gateway endpoints, Shield: unrelated to one instance's internet access.

Key takeaway: compare what differs between working and failing instances.

stem: Instances in a private subnet can successfully send outbound requests to an external API, but the responses never arrive back at the instances, even though the security group allows all outbound traffic and the security group's default stateful behavior should permit the return traffic. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The subnet's route table is missing a route to a NAT gateway
The NACL lacks an inbound rule for ephemeral return ports
The instances are not using Elastic IP addresses
The security group is missing an outbound rule

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Outbound requests succeed, so routing works. Responses return to ephemeral ports, which a stateless NACL must allow inbound.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Missing NAT route: requests would fail.
• Elastic IPs: not needed behind NAT.
• SG outbound rule: SGs are stateful.

Key takeaway: NACLs need return-port rules.

stem: An engineer is investigating why certain traffic to an EC2 instance is being dropped. They enable VPC Flow Logs on the relevant ENI and see log entries with the action field set to REJECT for the traffic in question. What does this indicate?

choices.text: A security group or NACL rule denied it
It was delivered, but the application returned an HTTP 4xx error
It was throttled due to instance CPU credit exhaustion
It was routed to the wrong Availability Zone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A REJECT record in flow logs means a security group or NACL denied the traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• HTTP 4xx: flow logs don't see HTTP.
• CPU credits: not a rejection.
• Wrong AZ: not a flow log status.

Key takeaway: REJECT = SG or NACL denial.

stem: Two VPCs, VPC-A and VPC-B, are both attached to the same AWS Transit Gateway. Instances in VPC-A can ping instances in a third VPC, VPC-C, also attached to the Transit Gateway, but VPC-A instances cannot reach VPC-B instances at all, despite security groups and NACLs allowing the traffic in both VPCs. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: The VPCs have overlapping CIDRs
Transit Gateway supports connectivity between only two VPCs at a time
VPC-B must be peered directly with VPC-A even when using Transit Gateway
A's TGW route table lacks B's route (association/propagation)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If VPC-A can't reach VPC-B, the TGW route table associated with A likely lacks B's route (missing association or propagation).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overlapping CIDRs: not indicated.
• Two-VPC limit: no.
• Peering required: no.

Key takeaway: TGW connectivity = association + propagation.

stem: Legitimate requests are being blocked by a web ACL. The team must identify which rule matched and see request details, then fix it without disabling the whole rule group. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Review VPC Flow Logs for the blocked requests
Check WAF logs; override that rule to Count
Check CloudTrail management events for WAF
Review Route 53 Resolver query logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
WAF logs (and sampled requests) show the terminating rule and action for each request. A rule action override to Count for the specific managed rule stops blocking while the rest of the group stays active.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: no HTTP detail.
• CloudTrail: API calls to configure WAF, not request evaluations.
• Resolver logs: DNS queries.

Key takeaway: find the rule in WAF logs; override narrowly.

stem: A company has a Site-to-Site VPN connection between its VPC and an on-premises data center using a virtual private gateway and dynamic (BGP) routing. On-premises servers can reach some VPC subnets but not others that were added to the VPC after the VPN was originally established. Static routing is not in use. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Site-to-Site VPN supports a maximum of two subnets per VPC
The virtual private gateway must be recreated for each new subnet
New CIDRs aren't advertised over BGP or propagated to route tables
BGP can't be used with Site-to-Site VPN, so switch to static routing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
New VPC CIDRs must be advertised over BGP and propagated to route tables. Otherwise on-premises can't reach them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two-subnet limit: no.
• Recreate VGW: no.
• BGP unsupported: supported.

Key takeaway: new CIDRs need advertisement and propagation.

stem: Users report intermittent 502 Bad Gateway errors when accessing an application through Amazon CloudFront, which uses an Application Load Balancer as its origin. The engineer wants to determine whether the errors originate from CloudFront, the ALB, or the backend targets. Which combination of logs provides the most complete picture?

choices.text: Route 53 query logs, since DNS issues are the main cause of 502 errors
Only AWS WAF logs, since 502 errors are always caused by WAF rules
CloudFront access logs plus ALB access logs
Only VPC Flow Logs, since they capture every HTTP status code

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront access logs show which requests got 502s, and ALB access logs show whether the origin returned the error.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DNS logs: not 502 causes.
• WAF logs only: not always WAF.
• Flow logs: no HTTP codes.

Key takeaway: trace 502s through each layer's logs.

stem: An operations team wants an alarm when memory utilization on Linux EC2 instances exceeds 85%. They cannot find a memory metric in the AWS/EC2 namespace. What should they do?

choices.text: Enable detailed monitoring on the instances.
Use the CPUUtilization metric as a proxy for memory.
The CloudWatch agent publishing memory metrics.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the instances' subnets.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EC2 doesn't publish memory metrics by default. The CloudWatch agent publishes memory utilization so you can alarm on it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Detailed monitoring: no memory metrics.
• CPU as proxy: inaccurate.
• Flow logs: network.

Key takeaway: memory alarms → CloudWatch agent.

stem: Request volume for an API varies strongly by hour and weekday. Static threshold alarms either fire every morning or miss real drops at night. Which alarm approach fits BEST?

choices.text: An anomaly detection alarm.
An alarm on the metric's Maximum statistic instead of Sum.
A static threshold alarm with a higher threshold.
Disable the alarms outside business hours.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Anomaly detection alarms learn hourly and weekly patterns and alert when values leave the expected band.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Maximum statistic: doesn't handle seasonality.
• Higher static threshold: misses issues.
• Disable off-hours: blind spots.

Key takeaway: seasonal metrics → anomaly detection.

stem: An RDS for PostgreSQL instance shows high CPU during business hours. The DBA needs to see which SQL statements and wait events contribute most to database load. Which tool fits BEST?

choices.text: CloudWatch CPUUtilization metric.
RDS Enhanced Monitoring.
AWS Trusted Advisor.
RDS Performance Insights.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Performance Insights shows which SQL statements drive database load and waits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CPU metric: no query detail.
• Enhanced Monitoring: OS metrics.
• Trusted Advisor: no.

Key takeaway: which SQL is expensive → Performance Insights.

stem: A company runs 600 EC2 instances and suspects many are over-provisioned. It wants right-sizing recommendations based on actual utilization, including memory where available. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: Compute Optimizer with agent memory metrics.
Amazon Inspector findings for each instance.
AWS Pricing Calculator estimates.
AWS Budgets alerts per instance family.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compute Optimizer recommends right-sizing, and including memory metrics from the CloudWatch agent makes recommendations more accurate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• Pricing Calculator: estimates.
• Budgets: spend alerts.

Key takeaway: right-sizing → Compute Optimizer + memory metrics.

stem: An application behind an ALB sometimes hangs while the EC2 instance itself keeps running. The ALB marks the target unhealthy, but the Auto Scaling group never replaces it. What should be changed?

choices.text: Enable detailed monitoring on the instances.
Set the group's health check type to ELB.
Disable cross-zone load balancing.
Increase the ALB idle timeout.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With the health check type set to ELB, the Auto Scaling group replaces instances that fail load balancer health checks, even if EC2 status checks pass.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Detailed monitoring: metrics only.
• Cross-zone: unrelated.
• Idle timeout: unrelated.

Key takeaway: replace app-unhealthy instances → ELB health checks.

stem: Backups of EC2, EBS, and RDS must be copied to another Region and another account, and must be protected so that no one, including administrators, can delete them before the retention period ends. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: EBS snapshots with a tag that says do not delete.
Backup plan with cross-Region/account copies to a Vault Lock vault.
S3 Versioning on the source account's buckets.
Manual snapshots copied by a nightly script.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An AWS Backup plan with cross-Region and cross-account copy rules to a vault protected by Vault Lock meets copy and immutability requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tags: not protection.
• S3 Versioning: not for EC2/EBS/RDS.
• Nightly scripts: fragile.

Key takeaway: protected cross-account backups → Backup + Vault Lock.

stem: A developer accidentally deleted rows from an RDS MySQL table at 14:05. Automated backups are enabled with 7-day retention. How can the operations team recover the data?

choices.text: Restore the existing instance in place to 14:04.
Promote a read replica to its state at 14:04.
Reboot the instance with failover to the standby.
Point-in-time restore to 14:04 (a new instance).

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Point-in-time restore to 14:04 creates a new instance with the data as of that time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• In-place restore: not supported.
• Promote replica: replica also has the deletion.
• Reboot with failover: same data.

Key takeaway: undo accidental deletes → PITR to a new instance.

stem: A content management system runs on EC2 instances in three Availability Zones behind an ALB. All instances must read and write the same uploaded files, and the storage must survive an AZ failure. Which storage fits BEST?

choices.text: Instance store volumes synchronized by rsync.
An EBS gp3 volume attached to one instance and shared over NFS.
An EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach across AZs.
Amazon EFS with mount targets in each AZ.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EFS with mount targets in each AZ provides a shared file system for instances across all three AZs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance store with rsync: fragile.
• EBS shared over NFS: single point of failure.
• io2 Multi-Attach across AZs: single AZ only.

Key takeaway: shared files across AZs → EFS.

stem: A company must patch 800 Windows and Linux instances monthly, approve only security updates released more than 7 days ago, patch production during a Sunday window, and report compliance. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: An EC2 user data script that updates on every boot.
Patch Manager with delayed-approval baselines, windows, and reporting.
Log in to each instance and run updates manually.
Replace instances with new AMIs every week.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Patch Manager with baselines that auto-approve security updates after a delay, maintenance windows, and compliance reporting handles 800 instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• User data on boot: uncontrolled.
• Manual: toil.
• Weekly AMI replacement: heavy for this.

Key takeaway: fleet patching → Patch Manager.

stem: A CloudFormation stack reports CREATE_COMPLETE for an EC2 instance before its user data script finishes installing the application, so dependent resources fail. What should the operations engineer add?

choices.text: A DeletionPolicy of Retain on the instance.
A CreationPolicy with cfn-signal.
A longer stack creation timeout.
A DependsOn attribute on the instance.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A CreationPolicy with cfn-signal makes CloudFormation wait for the instance to signal success after user data finishes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DeletionPolicy: deletion.
• Longer timeout: doesn't wait for signal.
• DependsOn: ordering only.

Key takeaway: wait for bootstrapping → CreationPolicy + cfn-signal.

stem: An engineer must restart a service on 300 instances tagged Role=web, at most 10% at a time, and stop if more than 5 instances fail. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: SSH into each instance with a loop script.
Use EC2 user data to restart the service.
Run Command by tag, 10% concurrency, 5-error threshold.
Reboot all instances from the console.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Run Command targeting the Role=web tag with 10% max concurrency and an error threshold of 5 restarts safely at scale.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSH loop: no controls.
• User data: runs at boot.
• Reboot all: disruptive.

Key takeaway: controlled fleet commands → Run Command rate controls.

stem: The team wants golden AMIs that are rebuilt automatically when new OS patches are released, hardened with CIS settings, tested, and distributed to three Regions. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: EC2 Image Builder pipelines.
Manual snapshots copied to three Regions.
CloudFormation drift detection on the AMI stacks.
AWS Backup AMI copies to three Regions.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EC2 Image Builder pipelines rebuild, harden, test, and distribute golden AMIs automatically on a schedule or on updates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual snapshots: not automated hardening.
• Drift detection: unrelated.
• Backup AMI copies: not rebuilding.

Key takeaway: golden AMI automation → Image Builder.

stem: An audit found that a developer made an S3 bucket public by mistake. Management wants to prevent any bucket in the account from becoming public through ACLs or bucket policies, including future buckets. What should be done?

choices.text: Enable default encryption on all buckets.
Enable S3 Versioning on all buckets.
Enable MFA Delete on all buckets.
Account-level S3 Block Public Access.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Account-level S3 Block Public Access prevents any bucket in the account from being made public.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default encryption: at rest.
• Versioning: recovery.
• MFA Delete: deletion protection.

Key takeaway: prevent public buckets → Block Public Access.

stem: A company with 30 accounts in several Regions wants one view of compliance for rules such as encrypted volumes and required tags. Which configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: Log in to each account and Region to check Config results.
Org-wide Config rules plus an aggregator.
Enable CloudTrail in each account and Region.
Use Trusted Advisor in the management account.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Org-wide Config rules (or conformance packs) plus an aggregator give one compliance view across accounts and Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual checks: toil.
• CloudTrail: API activity.
• Trusted Advisor: limited checks.

Key takeaway: multi-account compliance view → Config aggregator.

stem: A compliance standard requires encryption keys to be rotated regularly without re-encrypting existing data or changing application code. The data is encrypted with a KMS customer managed key. What should be done?

choices.text: Create a new key every year and re-encrypt all data manually.
Switch to SSE-S3 keys.
Enable automatic key rotation on the customer managed key.
Delete the key and let KMS generate a replacement.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automatic key rotation on a customer managed key creates new key material while old material still decrypts existing data, with no re-encryption needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual yearly re-encryption: unnecessary.
• SSE-S3: loses control.
• Delete key: loses data.

Key takeaway: rotate without re-encryption → KMS automatic rotation.

stem: A static site is served through CloudFront from a private S3 bucket. Users can currently bypass CloudFront by using the S3 URL directly. Which change ensures the bucket is only accessible through CloudFront?

choices.text: OAC plus a bucket policy for that distribution only.
Add a CloudFront custom header and leave S3 unchanged.
Enable static website hosting and make the bucket public.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Origin access control plus a bucket policy allowing only that distribution forces users to go through CloudFront.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom header only: bucket still reachable.
• Public website bucket: worse.
• Transfer Acceleration: unrelated.

Key takeaway: lock S3 to CloudFront → OAC.

stem: A Route 53 failover record uses a health check on an internal application that only has a private IP address in a VPC. The health check always reports unhealthy, even though the application works. What should be done?

choices.text: Change the record to simple routing.
Enable the health check's latency graphs.
Point the health check at the private IP with a shorter interval.
A health check based on a CloudWatch alarm.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Route 53 health checkers can't reach private IPs. Use a health check based on a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the internal application.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Simple routing: no failover.
• Latency graphs: no.
• Private IP health check: unreachable.

Key takeaway: private endpoints → alarm-based health checks.

stem: Instances in a private subnet cannot download updates. The private route table has 0.0.0.0/0 pointing to a NAT gateway. The NAT gateway was created in the same private subnet. What is the problem?

choices.text: The VPC must have DNS hostnames disabled.
The NAT gateway must be in a public subnet (IGW route).
NAT gateways require a security group allowing outbound traffic.
The instances need Elastic IP addresses.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A NAT gateway must be in a public subnet whose route table has a route to an internet gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DNS hostnames disabled: no.
• NAT gateway SGs: not applicable.
• Instance EIPs: not needed.

Key takeaway: NAT gateways live in public subnets.

stem: A web server in a public subnet can receive HTTPS requests, but responses never reach clients. Security groups allow inbound 443. The subnet's custom network ACL allows inbound 443 and outbound 443. What is missing?

choices.text: An outbound security group rule for port 443.
An Elastic IP address for the NAT gateway.
An inbound security group rule for ephemeral ports.
An outbound NACL rule for ephemeral ports.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups are stateful, but NACLs aren't. The subnet's NACL needs an outbound rule allowing ephemeral ports for responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outbound SG 443: SGs allow responses automatically.
• NAT EIP: unrelated.
• Inbound SG ephemeral: not needed.

Key takeaway: responses blocked → NACL outbound ephemeral rule.

stem: An ALB returns intermittent HTTP 502 errors. Target logs show the application server closes idle keep-alive connections after 5 seconds, while the ALB idle timeout is 60 seconds. What should the engineer do?

choices.text: Enable ALB access logs only.
Increase the number of registered targets.
App keep-alive longer than the ALB idle timeout.
Reduce the target group's health check interval.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the app closes idle keep-alive connections before the ALB does, the ALB can reuse a closed connection and return 502. Set the app keep-alive timeout longer than the ALB idle timeout.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access logs only: diagnosis, not fix.
• More targets: doesn't fix timeouts.
• Health check interval: unrelated.

Key takeaway: backend keep-alive > ALB idle timeout.
